compare.headline: Jianbing or Scallion Pancake?
differences: Crispy crepe folded around a crunchy wonton cracker
Flaky, layered pancake with 30+ paper-thin dough layers
Mung bean + wheat batter, cooked as a thin sheet
Saucy and savory with egg, bean paste, and scallions
Clean wheat flavor with scallion and lard
6-9 AM breakfast rush, eaten standing up
Morning or any time, sold all day
compare.chooseThisIf: You want a complete eggy breakfast that eats like a meal — or you're on a first visit and want the icon.
compare.chooseThatIf: You want a simpler, portable, less messy snack — or something crispier without sauce.

bestFor: First-time visitors who want China's most iconic street breakfast
Budget travelers — student-area jianbing costs ¥6-10
Early risers: best carts pack up by 9 AM
skipIf: You're craving something sweet, or you can't eat wheat or eggs. It's strictly savory.

compare.headline: Tanghulu or Bingfen?
differences: October to March — a winter street staple
May to September — a summer cooling dessert
Cold but crisp: hard sugar shell, tart fruit
Ice-cold jelly with brown sugar syrup
compare.chooseThisIf: You're visiting in winter and want the photogenic classic — or you love sour-sweet contrast.
compare.chooseThatIf: You're in Sichuan in summer and need a spicy-food fire extinguisher.

bestFor: Winter travelers in Beijing or Harbin
First-time visitors who want a famous, photogenic snack
People who like sour flavors (classic hawthorn version)
skipIf: You're visiting between April and September — most vendors are gone and the sugar melts. Also skip if you dislike sour fruit.

compare.headline: Xiaolongbao or Shengjian Bao?
differences: Steamed in bamboo baskets — delicate, translucent skin
Elegant: slurp the broth through a thin wrapper
Contrast: shatteringly crisp base, juicier pork
6:30-8:30 AM first batch, when the oil is clean
compare.chooseThisIf: You're a first-timer — it's easier to eat and the broth is cooler.
compare.chooseThatIf: You want more texture and richer flavor, and you can handle the heat.

bestFor: First-time visitors to Shanghai
Anyone who wants an elegant, easy-to-eat dumpling
Morning eaters on Yunnan Road
skipIf: You're in a hurry — it must be eaten fresh within 5 minutes of steaming. Skip if you're looking for something crispy.

compare.headline: Chuan Chuan or Mala Tang?
differences: Skewers you cook yourself in a boiling shared pot
A bowl of ingredients the cook boils for you
You manage cooking time for each skewer
You pick ingredients, the cook handles the rest
Count your sticks at the end — ¥0.5-1 each
By weight or by portion — ¥15-40 per bowl
compare.chooseThisIf: You're with friends and want a hands-on, interactive meal.
compare.chooseThatIf: You're alone or in a hurry and want the same flavors without the cooking.

bestFor: Groups who want a hands-on meal
Adventurous eaters ready for the Chengdu/Chongqing spice level
Budget travelers — counting sticks keeps costs transparent
skipIf: You're very sensitive to spice — even the 'mild' broth carries heat. Also skip if you dislike communal cooking pots.

compare.headline: Roujiamo or Yangrou Paomo?
differences: Fast street food — ready in minutes, eaten on the go
Ritual meal — you tear the bread yourself, then wait
Crispy flatbread stuffed with braised pork
Torn bread pieces simmered in lamb broth
compare.chooseThisIf: You want Xi'an's essential snack fast — the 'Chinese hamburger' experience.
compare.chooseThatIf: You have an hour and want the city's most immersive food ritual.

bestFor: First-timers in Xi'an — it's the fastest introduction to the city's food
Meat lovers who like slow-braised pork
Budget travelers wanting a filling lunch
skipIf: You're vegetarian — the classic version is pork. (Halal beef versions exist but are less common.)

compare.headline: Shengjian Bao or Xiaolongbao?
differences: Pan-fried: crispy golden bottom, soft top
Steamed: thin, translucent skin all around
Very hot — the frying seals in more moisture
compare.chooseThisIf: You want the most textural excitement and don't mind a first-bite burn risk.
compare.chooseThatIf: You're a first-timer or want something easier and more elegant to eat.

bestFor: Breakfast purists — the first batch at 6:30 AM is the best batch
People who love crispy textures
Shanghai first-timers who want the city's street-level classic
skipIf: You can't eat it fresh — cold shengjian bao lose all their crunch within minutes.

compare.headline: Mala Tang or Chuan Chuan?
differences: Bowl of boiled ingredients, cooked for you
DIY skewers you cook in a shared pot
Zero technique — just pick and wait
Individual bowl, perfect for solo diners
¥0.5-1 per stick, count at the end
compare.chooseThisIf: You're dining solo or want a fast, no-fuss spicy meal.
compare.chooseThatIf: You're with friends and want the interactive version.

bestFor: Solo travelers
Vegetarians — easy to pick a meat-free bowl
First-timers to Sichuan spice, since you control the ingredients
skipIf: You dislike DIY assembly and want a sit-down meal — or you're avoiding spice entirely.

compare.chooseThisIf: You want a free crunchy palate reset between spicy bites — and a signal the kitchen cares.
compare.chooseThatIf: You want a proper cold meal that stands on its own.
differences: Free side dish served before or with your meal
Free — quality is the restaurant's pride signal
¥8-18 at Wei Jia Liangpi and similar shops
Alongside the meal, keeps the palate fresh
At lunch, as the meal itself

bestFor: Anyone eating Sichuan food — it's free and included
Vegetarians and vegans
People who like pickled, sour flavors
skipIf: You're not eating at a Sichuan restaurant — it's rarely sold as a standalone street snack.

compare.chooseThisIf: You want something cold, filling, and tangy — a proper lunch in itself, not a side.
compare.chooseThatIf: You want a free, instant palate reset while you figure out what to actually order.
differences: A full cold lunch — noodles, cucumber, chili oil
A free side dish — a few crunchy bites between courses
Slippery chewy noodles cut with cucumber crunch
Sour brine with Sichuan peppercorn heat
Free at nearly every Sichuan restaurant

bestFor: Summer visitors to Xi'an
Vegetarians — the classic version is meat-free
Anyone who wants a quick lunch that won't weigh them down
skipIf: You're gluten-sensitive — liangpi is made from wheat or rice starch but usually handled with wheat flour.

compare.headline: Dan Dan Mian or Chongqing Xiaomian?
differences: Chengdu: layered, fragrant chili oil with sesame paste
Chongqing: aggressive, immediate, darker roasted chili
Often simpler — noodles, greens, chili, pepper
Jinli or Chen Mapo Tofu on Qingyang Street
compare.chooseThisIf: You want to taste Sichuan's layered, balanced chili oil artistry.
compare.chooseThatIf: You want the spicier, bolder street version — and can handle it.

bestFor: First-timers to Sichuan noodles — it's the approachable entry point
Anyone who wants a full, saucy meal in a bowl
Fans of sesame-based sauces
skipIf: You're spice-averse — even 'mild' carries chili oil. Ask for wei la and be ready anyway.

compare.headline: Bingfen or Tanghulu?
differences: May to September — summer cooling dessert
October to March — winter street staple
Cold jelly that resets the palate after spice
Crisp sugar shell cracking over tart fruit
compare.chooseThisIf: You just ate spicy food and need a cold, gentle reset — or it's summer.
compare.chooseThatIf: You're in the north in winter and want the seasonal icon.

bestFor: Anyone eating Sichuan hot pot — the traditional finishing move
Summer travelers
Vegetarians and vegans
skipIf: You're visiting between October and March — bingfen stalls mostly disappear outside summer.

compare.chooseThisIf: It's evening and you want to graze — skewers, cold beer, and a crowd.
compare.chooseThatIf: It's lunchtime and you need one filling, seated meal before afternoon sightseeing.
differences: A single bowl, eaten fast at lunch
Savory fermented soybean paste with pork and cucumber
Evening, when the grills fire up
Lunch — 11:30 AM to 1:30 PM is classic
¥3-8 per skewer, count as you go

bestFor: Night-market lovers — the Muslim Quarter at 6 PM is the peak moment
Anyone who loves cumin
Groups sharing food
skipIf: You're vegetarian — or you're in a hurry (skewers are best eaten slowly, skewer after skewer).

compare.chooseThisIf: You want one hot, filling, sit-down bowl at lunch — the Beijing classic.
compare.chooseThatIf: You want a snack-style evening crawl with smoke and cumin.
differences: A complete bowl — noodles, dark amber sauce, fresh vegetables
Skewers — order 10, count sticks at the end
Deep fermented soybean paste, savory and slightly sweet
Charcoal-smoked lamb with cumin and chili
Lunch, when the sauce is freshly cooked
Evening, when the grills light up

bestFor: People who want authentic Beijing flavor without spice
Fans of fermented bean paste (miso-like depth)
Lunch eaters near universities for student prices
skipIf: You're craving heat — this is a no-chili dish by tradition.

compare.chooseThisIf: You're eating with rice and want the signature sharing dish of Sichuan.
compare.chooseThatIf: You want a lighter, softer bite where vinegar balances the heat.
differences: A main dish — tofu in numbing chili oil, eaten over rice
Wontons — 10 soft parcels under red chili oil
Numbing (ma) forward — Sichuan peppercorn is the star
Spicy, with black vinegar cutting the burn
Share it — it's a table dish
A snack or light meal for one
Chen Mapo Tofu on Qingyang Street

bestFor: Anyone eating their first Sichuan meal — it's the classic benchmark
Tofu lovers
People who want a dish with rice
skipIf: You're a strict vegetarian — the traditional version includes ground pork in the sauce (ask for su version).

compare.headline: Chongqing Xiaomian or Dan Dan Mian?
differences: Extreme — the deep end of Sichuan spice
Chongqing, where mild means something else
compare.chooseThisIf: You've built some tolerance and want the most intense noodle experience in China.
compare.chooseThatIf: You're new to Sichuan food and want layers you can actually taste.

bestFor: Spice enthusiasts — Chongqing is the deep end
Budget travelers — the cheapest serious meal in town
Breakfast eaters who like noodles at 8 AM
skipIf: You're spice-sensitive — even 'bu la' (no spice) requests may earn confusion.

compare.chooseThisIf: You want a light, silky savory bite to start the day.
compare.chooseThatIf: You want the sweet afternoon break — the 2:45 PM batch at Lian Xiang Lou.
differences: Savory steamed rice noodle rolls — breakfast
Silky, slippery sheets with soy-sesame sauce
Around 3 PM, when the fresh batch comes out

bestFor: Breakfast lovers in Guangzhou
People who prefer soft, slippery textures
Vegetarians — plain cheong fun with soy sauce works
skipIf: You want something with chew and bite — cheong fun is deliberately soft.

compare.headline: Egg Tart or Cheong Fun?
differences: Around 3 PM, when the fresh batch comes out
compare.chooseThisIf: You want a sweet afternoon break — grab it at Lian Xiang Lou when the 2:45 PM batch is fresh.
compare.chooseThatIf: You're hungry for something savory and filling.

bestFor: Afternoon snackers
Anyone with a sweet tooth
Fans of Portuguese-style pastries wanting the Cantonese take
skipIf: You're looking for a meal, not a treat — an egg tart is a moment, not a lunch.

compare.chooseThisIf: You want one light, saucy bite that's spicy but balanced by vinegar.
compare.chooseThatIf: You're eating a proper meal with rice and want the classic sharing dish.
differences: 10 wontons in red chili oil — a snack or light meal
A main dish of silken tofu over rice
Chili oil + black vinegar — bright and sharp
Numbing chili oil — thick, earthy, peppercorn-forward
Built to share with rice and cold drinks
Chen Mapo Tofu on Qingyang Street

bestFor: People who like dumplings and want to try them Sichuan-style
Lighter eaters
Fans of chili oil with a vinegar counterpoint
skipIf: You're very hungry — 10 wontons may not cut it. Order two servings or add noodles.

compare.headline: Yangrou Paomo or Roujiamo?
differences: You tear the bread yourself — the smaller, the better
A warming winter meal in a bowl
compare.chooseThisIf: It's cold, you have an hour, and you want Xi'an's most immersive food ritual.
compare.chooseThatIf: You're on the move and need something fast and filling.

bestFor: Winter visitors to Xi'an — it's the city's ultimate comfort food
Anyone who loves interactive food experiences
Halal eaters — it's lamb and bread, no pork
skipIf: You're in a rush — the bread-tearing ritual can't be rushed, and neither should the meal.

compare.headline: Scallion Pancake or Jianbing?
differences: Flaky, layered, crispy all the way through
Soft crepe with one crunchy cracker layer
None — clean wheat, scallion, and lard flavor

compare.chooseThatIf: You want the full saucy breakfast experience.

compare.chooseThisIf: You want a complete meal — noodles, wontons, and broth with real depth.
compare.chooseThatIf: You're at a dim sum table and want the craft test of the kitchen.
